_comment: In-game encyclopedia (Codex, J). Terms unlock when a briefing, event walkthrough or report first mentions them. 'game' = where it shows up in this game. Keep 'body' short: it is drawn at 8 px on a 480x270 screen.

delta_v.name: Delta-v (dv)
delta_v.body: How much a spacecraft can change its speed with the fuel it carries, in km/s. Every manoeuvre costs some. More mass needs more fuel for the same delta-v - so fuel is mass.
delta_v.game: The launch and every Navigator burn spend it. Heavy ships need bigger rockets.

hohmann.name: Hohmann transfer
hohmann.body: The cheapest path between two orbits: half an ellipse touching Earth's orbit at one end and Mars' at the other. Earth to Mars takes about 259 days this way.
hohmann.game: The standard path. Faster paths cost more fuel.

launch_window.name: Launch window
launch_window.body: Earth and Mars line up for a cheap transfer only about every 26 months. Miss the window and you wait two years - or pay a lot more fuel.
launch_window.game: Why every mission has a fixed launch date.

max_q.name: Max-Q
max_q.body: The moment of greatest aerodynamic stress on a climbing rocket: speed is high and the air is still thick. Rockets throttle down through it.
max_q.game: The launch mini-game: too much throttle = stress = breakup.

dynamic_pressure.name: Dynamic pressure (q)
dynamic_pressure.body: The push of the air on a moving rocket: q = 1/2 x air density x speed squared. Twice as fast = four times the push. Air thins with height, so q peaks low and fast.
dynamic_pressure.game: The STRESS bar during the launch. The failure report graphs it.

thrust_to_weight.name: Thrust-to-weight
thrust_to_weight.body: Engine thrust divided by the rocket's weight. Below 1 the rocket can't rise at all; only the thrust above its weight speeds it up. A heavier payload lowers it.
thrust_to_weight.game: The green LIFT mark on the throttle lever.

rocket_equation.name: Rocket equation
rocket_equation.body: Speed a rocket can gain = exhaust speed x ln(full mass / empty mass). Payload counts as empty mass, so a heavier payload means less speed. Real rockets are about 85-90% fuel at liftoff.
rocket_equation.game: Why a heavy ship needs a bigger rocket, and why staging helps.

gravity_loss.name: Gravity loss
gravity_loss.body: While a rocket climbs, part of its thrust only holds it up against gravity. Orbit is 7.8 km/s, but getting there takes about 9.4 km/s - the rest goes to gravity and air drag.
gravity_loss.game: Climbing at low throttle wastes fuel. The launch report shows how much.

staging.name: Staging
staging.body: Dropping an empty rocket stage so the rest doesn't carry its dead weight. Almost every orbital rocket does it.
staging.game: SPACE at stage 1 burnout during the launch.

mars_orbit_insertion.name: Mars Orbit Insertion (MOI)
mars_orbit_insertion.body: The braking burn when a spacecraft reaches Mars. Too little and it flies past; too low and it hits the atmosphere. It must work the first time, on its own - Earth is minutes away by radio.
mars_orbit_insertion.game: The Navigator HOLDS the brake at the end. Needs fuel AND power.

aerobraking.name: Aerobraking
aerobraking.body: Dipping again and again into the top of a planet's atmosphere so drag slowly lowers the orbit - saving fuel. Odyssey made 332 passes over 77 days; MRO aerobraked about 5 months.
aerobraking.game: The AEROBRAKE orbit: a small brake burn, then months before science starts.

polar_orbit.name: Low polar orbit
polar_orbit.body: A low, round orbit that crosses over both poles. As the planet turns underneath, the spacecraft sees every part of it. Odyssey maps Mars from about 400 km up.
polar_orbit.game: LOW POLAR orbit: most science, biggest brake burn, short contact with Earth.

elliptical_orbit.name: Elliptical orbit
elliptical_orbit.body: An oval orbit: close to the planet at one end, far away at the other. Cheaper to brake into than a low round orbit. MAVEN flies between about 150 and 6,200 km above Mars.
elliptical_orbit.game: HIGH ELLIPTICAL orbit: cheap brake, long contact with Earth, fewer close looks.

dsn.name: Deep Space Network (DSN)
dsn.body: NASA's giant antennas in California (Goldstone), Spain (Madrid) and Australia (Canberra), about 120 degrees apart, so one always faces the spacecraft as Earth turns.
dsn.game: Comms can only send data during a DSN pass (bottom right).

downlink.name: Downlink
downlink.body: Sending data from the spacecraft down to Earth. Uplink is the other way. Data rate drops with distance and depends on antenna size and power.
downlink.game: Comms HOLDS SPACE. Only SENT science scores.

high_gain_antenna.name: High-gain antenna
high_gain_antenna.body: A big dish that focuses the radio beam into a narrow cone: much faster data, but it must point precisely at Earth. MRO's dish is 3 m across.
high_gain_antenna.game: COM upgrade: faster downlink, costs mass and power.

light_time_delay.name: Light-time delay
light_time_delay.body: Radio travels at light speed, but Mars is far: a signal takes 4 to 24 minutes one way. Nobody on Earth can steer a Mars spacecraft live.
light_time_delay.game: Why the crew (and real probes) must handle problems themselves.

solar_conjunction.name: Solar conjunction
solar_conjunction.body: About every 26 months the Sun passes between Earth and Mars. Its radio noise blocks contact for roughly two weeks, so missions stop sending commands.
solar_conjunction.game: MRO mission: a comms blackout. Empty the recorder before it.

solar_particle_event.name: Solar particle event
solar_particle_event.body: A burst of fast protons from a solar flare or eruption. It can damage electronics and is the biggest radiation danger to astronauts beyond Earth's magnetic field.
solar_particle_event.game: The radiation storm: a warning, then the wave.

solar_wind.name: Solar wind
solar_wind.body: A constant stream of charged particles flowing out from the Sun at hundreds of km/s, filling the whole solar system.
solar_wind.game: MAVEN mission: what strips Mars' air.

safe_mode.name: Safe mode
safe_mode.body: When something goes wrong, real spacecraft switch off non-essential systems, point at the Sun for power and wait for help from Earth. It protects the craft but stops science.
safe_mode.game: Engineer's breaker minigame before a storm without shielding.

radiation_dose.name: Radiation dose (mSv)
radiation_dose.body: How much radiation energy a body absorbs, weighted for harm, in millisieverts. On Earth we get about 2-3 mSv a year. Curiosity measured about 1.8 mSv PER DAY on its cruise to Mars. NASA's career limit for an astronaut is 600 mSv.
radiation_dose.game: Each astronaut's dose bar, bottom left. Past 500 mSv they get radiation sickness and work slower (SIMPLIFIED).

storm_shelter.name: Storm shelter
storm_shelter.body: During a solar storm, Orion's crew moves into the middle of the capsule and walls themselves in with stowage bags. On Artemis I, a sensor in the shelter measured about half the dose of the main cabin.
storm_shelter.game: The CARGO bay. No shields? Everyone must be inside when the wave hits.

eva.name: Spacewalk (EVA)
eva.body: Extravehicular activity: going outside in a pressurised suit, tethered to the ship, moving hand over hand along handrails. Crews have fixed things robots could not: in 2007 an astronaut repaired a torn ISS solar wing, in 2013 two spacewalkers stopped an ammonia coolant leak. A robot probe can't - Galileo's big dish never opened in 1991. Outside there is no air, so no sound, and no shelter from radiation. A suit lasts about 8 hours.
eva.game: Faults on the outside of the ship: suit up at the BRIDGE AIRLOCK, walk the hull, HOLD SPACE at the job, come back before the suit O2 runs out (SIMPLIFIED: 75 s).

flight_plan.name: Flight plan + stored commands
flight_plan.body: Probes can't wait for orders: radio takes minutes to reach Mars. Teams plan weeks ahead and upload stored command sequences that run on their own - a flyby of an asteroid, a trajectory correction, heater settings. Galileo met the asteroids Gaspra (1991) and Ida (1993) this way, Rosetta met Steins (2008) and Lutetia (2010).
flight_plan.game: The Mission Hub holo-table: plan comet trails, asteroid flybys, the cold zone and the conjunction before the ship gets there.

near_earth_asteroid.name: Near-Earth asteroid
near_earth_asteroid.body: Rocky bodies whose orbits come close to Earth's; some reach out past Mars. Spacecraft have visited several: NEAR landed on 433 Eros (2001), Hayabusa and Hayabusa2 brought dust home from Itokawa and Ryugu, OSIRIS-REx brought a sample of Bennu (2023). Space between the planets is mostly empty - real flybys are planned, not dodged.
near_earth_asteroid.game: Asteroids on the flight plan: plan a flyby and the Scientist gets a 2x science window.

comet_debris.name: Comet debris
comet_debris.body: Comets leave trails of dust and grit along their orbits (Earth's meteor showers come from them). Grains hit at tens of km/s. In this game the chunks are exaggerated.
comet_debris.game: Bridge radar: steer around it or fly through (SIMPLIFIED).

radiation_shielding.name: Radiation shielding
radiation_shielding.body: Mass between the crew and space - water, polyethylene, the hull - that stops particles. It works, but every kilogram must be launched.
radiation_shielding.game: PWR upgrade, 50 kg: raise it at the Mission Hub table.

rad_hard.name: Radiation-hardened computer
rad_hard.body: Chips built to survive particle hits that would flip bits in normal electronics. Slower and far more expensive than a laptop chip.
rad_hard.game: PWR upgrade: fewer faults, easier storm minigames.

rtg.name: RTG
rtg.body: Radioisotope thermoelectric generator: heat from decaying plutonium-238 becomes electricity. Works in darkness and storms. Curiosity and Perseverance use one.
rtg.game: PWR upgrade: power that survives a blackout.

whipple_shield.name: Whipple shield
whipple_shield.body: A thin bumper layer spaced out from the hull: a particle shatters on it and spreads out before reaching the wall. Used on the ISS.
whipple_shield.game: NAV upgrade: halves debris damage, fewer breaches.

hull_breach.name: Hull breach
hull_breach.body: A hole in a pressurised hull. Air escapes into vacuum; small leaks give the crew time to find and patch them. The ISS has had small leaks patched by its crew.
hull_breach.game: Toolbox from a red locker, HOLD SPACE on the hole.

hirise.name: HiRISE
hirise.body: The High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment on MRO: a telescope camera that sees objects about 1 m wide from orbit. Its images are enormous files.
hirise.game: MRO mission: why the recorder fills so fast.

marie.name: MARIE
marie.body: The Mars Radiation Environment Experiment on Mars Odyssey. It measured space radiation to prepare for human missions until a huge solar storm knocked it out in October 2003.

magnetosphere.name: Magnetosphere
magnetosphere.body: The bubble a planet's magnetic field makes around it. Earth's deflects the solar wind. Mars lost its global field about 4 billion years ago.
magnetosphere.game: MAVEN mission: why Mars lost its air.

atmospheric_escape.name: Atmospheric escape
atmospheric_escape.body: Gas leaking off the top of an atmosphere into space. MAVEN measured Mars losing about 100 g every second to the solar wind - more during solar storms.
atmospheric_escape.game: MAVEN mission: measure storms hitting Mars.

au.name: Astronomical unit (AU)
au.body: The average Earth-Sun distance, about 150 million km. Mars orbits at about 1.52 AU, so sunlight there is only ~43% as strong.
au.game: Top left of the HUD: the ship gets darker as you fly out.
